title: Grožnjan First-Time Visitor Guide & Tips 2027
metaDescription: Plan a first visit to Grožnjan, Istria's hilltop artists' town: when to go, parking, galleries, festivals, food, distances and insider tips for 2027.
content:
## How to Get to Grožnjan

Grožnjan sits on a hill above the Mirna river valley in the northwest of Istria. A car is the practical way to reach it. Public transport is limited and infrequent, and the town has no train station.

- **From Novigrad:** about 20 km, roughly 25 minutes.
- **From Motovun:** about 17 km.
- **From Poreč:** about 35–40 km, under an hour.
- **From Pula:** about 80 km, roughly 1 hour 15 minutes.
- **From Trieste (Italy):** about 60 km via the Slovenian border area; carry a passport or ID card.

The old town is largely car-free. Park in the lots at the foot of the hill and walk up. Parking is paid in season, with the cost typically a few euros for a half-day. Bring coins or a card in case the machine is temperamental.

## How Long to Spend in Grožnjan

Two to three hours covers the old town, a gallery or two and a coffee. Add an hour for lunch. A full day only makes sense if a concert is on in the evening. Grožnjan is small, with about 100 permanent residents in the old core, so the streets stay quiet outside festival periods.

The town works best as one stop in a hill-town day. A common combination is Grožnjan, Motovun and a truffle lunch in Livade. Guided day tours from Rovinj, Poreč and Pula follow the same pattern.

## What Makes Grožnjan Different

After World War II, the Italian population left and the town was nearly abandoned. In the 1960s, artists and musicians took over empty stone houses and turned them into studios. Grožnjan was formally designated a town of artists in 1965, and it now has around 20 galleries and studios.

The castle, first mentioned in 1102, houses the International Cultural Centre of Jeunesses Musicales Croatia. From May to October, music students rehearse in the town's halls and classrooms, and practice drifts out of open windows.

## Best Things to Do in Grožnjan

### Walk the Old Town

Enter through the 15th-century town gate. Its outer face carries the coats of arms of Venetian administrators. The main lanes can be walked end to end in 15 minutes, so the point is to go slowly and look into doorways. The Belvedere terrace at the edge of town has the best views across the Mirna valley toward the Motovun hill.

### Visit the Fonticus Gallery

The Fonticus occupies the Venetian loggia built in 1597. It runs solo exhibitions and visual art projects throughout the year and shows work from the town's own art holdings. It is the best first stop if you want to see what the local artists' circle produces.

### Browse the Private Galleries and Studios

Studios sell paintings, ceramics, textiles, jewellery and woodwork. Quality varies. Some shops sell mass-produced souvenirs, including imported items, so ask the person behind the counter whether the work is their own. Studios that are staffed by the artist are the ones worth buying from. Many owners open irregularly and close for lunch or on quiet weekdays outside summer.

### See the Churches

The parish church of St Vitus, Modestus and Crescentius dates to 1600 and has Baroque choir stalls. Its bell tower is 36 m high. The small chapel of St Cosmas and Damian, from 1554, has a porch of the 'lopica' type. Check Spinotti Palace from outside for its Baroque façade.

## Best Time to Visit Grožnjan

May to October is the practical season, when studios are most often open and music courses run. Opinion: **mid-July and late September are the two best windows**, because the town then has a programme rather than just scenery.

- **Jazz is Back B.P. (mid-July):** a two-week festival of nightly open-air concerts, jam sessions and a summer jazz school, founded by Boško Petrović in 1999. Concerts have been staged at the Balwan City summer stage and the Belvedere, with Istrian wine and olive oil tastings alongside.
- **Ex Tempore (last weekend of September):** an international painting event held since 1994. The programme opens on Thursday with canvas stamping and ends with an awards ceremony on Sunday. Painters work in lanes and loggias all over town.
- **Winter:** most galleries and cafés are closed or on short hours. Go only if you want a silent village.

August midday is hot on exposed stone. Visit before 11:00 or after 17:00.

## Where to Eat and Drink

Grožnjan's food is inland Istrian: fuži or pici pasta, truffles, pršut, local cheese, olive oil and Malvazija white wine or Teran red. Truffle season peaks in autumn for white truffles, while black truffles are available for much of the year.

- **Zigante Enoteka (Gorjan 5):** a small deli in the old town selling truffle products, cheese, olive oils and local wines. You can sit for a glass of wine and a plate of savoury snacks.
- **Konoba Tre Volti:** a traditional Istrian restaurant, rated 4.5 on Tripadvisor.
- **Amodomio:** a pizza and Italian place, rated 3.7, more casual and with a lower rating than the konobas.
- **Konoba Pintur:** a konoba on Ulica Mate Gorjana.

For a bigger truffle meal, drive to Zigante in Livade or Konoba Mondo in Motovun. Budget about €15–25 for a main course in a konoba. Truffle dishes cost significantly more, often €25–40 depending on the truffle weight. Always ask the price of shaved truffle before ordering.

## Insider Tips for First-Time Visitors

1. **Wear flat shoes.** The stone is polished and slippery, especially after rain.
2. **Arrive early in July.** Jazz evenings fill the cafés and parking lots by early evening. Book dinner in advance on concert nights.
3. **Carry some cash.** Small galleries and cafés sometimes prefer cards only above a minimum, or not at all.
4. **Listen for rehearsals.** Daytime student concerts in summer are often free and informal.
5. **Pair it with the Parenzana.** The former narrow-gauge railway line, now a greenway, passes close to the town and works for cycling.
6. **Fill up the tank first.** Rural Istria has few fuel stations outside the bigger towns.
7. **Combine with wine.** Local wineries around Grožnjan and Motovun, including Fakin, offer tastings; call ahead.

## Where to Stay

The old town has only a few rooms and apartments, and many visitors stay in surrounding villages, agritourism farms or coastal bases. Umag, Novigrad and Poreč are the usual coastal bases, each within about 20–40 km. Inland, Motovun is 17 km away. Staying overnight in Grožnjan itself gives you the quiet evening streets once the day-trip groups have left.

## Is Grožnjan Worth Visiting?

Yes, if you value atmosphere, galleries and music over landmarks. It is not a town with a major monument and it is not large enough for a full day without an event. Treat it as a half-day stop and time it with a festival, and it is one of the better hill-town visits in Istria.

faq.question: How much time do you need in Grožnjan?
faq.answer: Two to three hours is enough for the old town, galleries and a coffee. Add an hour for lunch, or stay into the evening if a concert is scheduled.

faq.question: Is Grožnjan worth visiting?
faq.answer: Yes, for galleries, quiet cobbled lanes and valley views, especially during Jazz is Back in July or Ex Tempore in September. It has no large monuments, so it works best as a half-day stop combined with Motovun or Livade.

faq.question: How do you get to Grožnjan without a car?
faq.answer: Public transport is limited, so a car is the most practical option. Guided day tours from Rovinj, Poreč and Pula include Grožnjan, often with Motovun and a truffle tasting.

faq.question: When is the best time to visit Grožnjan?
faq.answer: May to October is the best period, when studios are open and music courses are running. Mid-July is the peak time for jazz, and the last weekend of September is the time for the Ex Tempore painting festival.

faq.question: How far is Grožnjan from Poreč, Motovun and Pula?
faq.answer: Grožnjan is about 20 km from Novigrad, 17 km from Motovun, around 35–40 km from Poreč and roughly 80 km from Pula. Driving times range from about 20 minutes to 1 hour 15 minutes.

faq.question: Is Grožnjan expensive?
faq.answer: No. Entry to the old town and churches is free, and a konoba main course is typically €15–25. Truffle dishes and festival tickets push the cost higher.

faq.question: What is Grožnjan famous for?
faq.answer: It is known as the town of artists, with about 20 galleries and studios, plus the Jeunesses Musicales music centre. It is also known for the Jazz is Back B.P. festival and the Ex Tempore painting event.

quickAnswer: Grožnjan is a hilltop artists' town in inland Istria, about 20 km from Novigrad and 17 km from Motovun. Allow 2–3 hours. Arrive by car, park outside the old centre, and walk the cobbled lanes and galleries. Visit May–October, ideally in mid-July for Jazz is Back or late September for Ex Tempore.
